transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Recorded: yes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Miles Ortega (Redwood SE), Kavita Das (Redwood CE), Priya Nair (Aureum SRE), Tomás Ruiz (Aureum ML Infra), Aisha Khan (Aureum Eng Mgr), Benji Lee (Aureum DS)

Summary:
Quick deep dive to triage a reproducible slowdown and occasional nondeterministic latency spikes that Aureum saw when moving a 7B-ish decoder model to their private VPC cluster. Suspected interactions: persistent KV cache eviction/prefetch, CUDA graph capture/replay, and kernel selection fallbacks between TensorRT-LLM fused kernels and vLLM dynamic kernels. Goal: create deterministic captures and run a 3-config microbenchmark (hosted-like/optimized, private default, private with prefetch tuned) to isolate root cause and suggest mitigations.

Topics covered:
- Observed symptom patterns and when spikes happen (prefetch heavy workloads, mixed sequence lengths)
- Kernel selection heuristics in Redwood runtime and how our fallback triggers (memory contention, unsupported kernels, cudagraph replay mismatch)
- Differences in execution between TensorRT-LLM optimized paths and vLLM dynamic scheduling for heterogeneous batches
- How KV cache prefetch/pinning interacts with CUDA graph capture and pinned memory lifetimes
- Quantization edge cases (int8 / q4 variants) and their interaction with TRT kernels and cudagraph replay
- VPC/on-prem constraints: NUMA, driver versions, and security constraints that limit debug tooling

Transcript:
[00:00] Laura Chen: ok everyone thanks for joining, we have 75 minutes on the book. We'll start with Aureum's symptom, then I'll hand off to Miles to explain what we've been seeing in the runtime traces, and then we'll do triage steps and next steps.

[00:38] Priya Nair: thanks. quick context: we moved the model from hosted test to our private cluster last month. most tokens are fine, but during high-concurrency peaks we see 2x-3x tail lat spikes for some requests. it's intermittent, and correlates with a particular prompt mix — lots of short-turn memory lookups and a few long context expansions.

[01:20] Tomás Ruiz: adding, it's on a heterogeneous NVLink cluster: two A100-SXM40 + two Ampere L40s. driver is 525.xx, CUDA 11.8. we tried pinning to an all-A100 node and still saw spikes.

[02:05] Miles Ortega: ok thanks. we pulled the traces you gave — thanks for uploading — and there are a few recurring patterns. first, kernel dispatch sometimes hits an unsupported fused kernel path (we'll call it TRT-fused) and falls back to a slower dynamic kernel path the next iteration. second, when KV prefetch tries to repopulate caches concurrently with cudagraph replay, there are mismatches in buffer lifetimes that force a graph replay and extra synchronization. both can produce ms-scale jitter.

[03:15] Aisha Khan: can you explain the "graph replay" bit? we thought cudagraphs were static captures and should be deterministic.

[03:37] Miles Ortega: good question. cudagraph capture captures a sequence of CUDA launches for a given set of buffer addresses and shapes. if any address / memory registration changes between capture and replay, or if a kernel path switch occurs (say the TRT kernel isn't available because a weight permutation wasn't aligned), the runtime will invalidate and re-capture — that's the replay. re-capture itself is heavier and it also changes the timing profile because some async prefetches are serialized during capture.

[04:42] Benji Lee: so are you saying KV prefetch can move a buffer around and cause the addresses to shift? that sounds... surprising.

[05:05] Miles Ortega: it can. especially when prefetch uses a pinned staging buffer or when the OS/driver places pages differently after memory pressure. one pattern we saw: persistent KV cache eviction triggers an allocation pattern that moves pinned buffers to a different address space; when cudagraph replay expects the old addresses, mismatch triggers re-capture.

[06:28] Priya Nair: our infra team also saw gds pinned mem churn during a big backfill. we didn't correlate it to cudagraphs until you flagged it.

[07:00] Laura Chen: high level mitigation options: (1) make prefetch deterministic with stable pinned buffers (we can pin a large slab and sub-allocate), (2) force kernel-path lockstep for critical routes (prefer TRT path and refuse to fallback unless explicitly allowed), (3) fall back gracefully with a short-circuit to a lightweight fast-path that preserves graph addresses. each has trade-offs.

[07:45] Tomás Ruiz: what's the risk of locking to TRT kernels? we tried TRT for perf but saw lower accuracy on q4 variants in an earlier test.

[08:10] Miles Ortega: TRT fused kernels assume certain weight layouts and quantization kernels. with q4 variants or certain per-channel scales we sometimes need an alternative kernel. locking to TRT is only safe if we pre-verify the exact kernel compatibility for the model/quantization. otherwise you get correctness issues or you'll reject requests that don't match.

[09:05] Aisha Khan: how does vLLM compare here? we were evaluating it as a reference runtime, it seemed more stable but slightly higher median latency.

[09:30] Miles Ortega: vLLM tends to have a dynamic execution path that handles heterogenous sequence lengths and kv-access patterns more gracefully. it doesn't rely as heavily on cudagraphs for micro-ops, so it's less sensitive to address churn from prefetch. downside: more scheduler overhead and per-token dispatch so median increases. TRT-LLM with static fused kernels gets lower median when everything lines up but is brittle under memory churn.

[10:45] Priya Nair: any numbers you can share from your lab? helps us set expectations.

[11:08] Miles Ortega: prototypical numbers on a single A100 for the customer's 7B-ish model (mixed prompts):
- TRT-fused path (FP16, q8-ish): median ~1.6ms/token, p95 ~2.0ms
- vLLM dynamic path (FP16): median ~2.4ms/token, p95 ~3.2ms
- When graph replay is triggered intermittently, TRT path p95 can jump to 6-10ms for affected requests due to capture overhead
these are lab numbers but align with what we see in traces. also quantization to int8 with calibration either worsens fallback frequency (more kernel incompatibility) or improves throughput when supported natively.

[13:00] Tomás Ruiz: interesting. we use q4_k standard for most models. does TRT support q4_k well?

[13:24] Miles Ortega: TRT has patchy support: some fused kernels support symmetric q4 variants, others require a dequant step. that's the root of some path switches — runtime prefers fused, but if dequant needed it opts out.

[14:02] Kavita Das: to add, there's also interactions with NUMA. on multi-socket machines, if prefetch touches a different NUMA node than capture, the physical page addresses can differ. that produces the same symptom as buffer move.

[15:10] Priya Nair: ok practical ask: what can we do immediately to reduce spikes while you investigate?

[15:30] Laura Chen: immediate mitigations (low friction):
- Increase prefetch backoff threshold so prefetch doesn't run during bursty short prompts (targets those short-turn memory lookups)
- Temporarily disable cudagraphs for routes that see frequent KV churn (fallback to vLLM-style dynamic)
- Reserve a pinned slab for KV prefetch allocations (we can provide a script)
these reduce spikes but may increase median slightly.

[16:50] Benji Lee: if we disable cudagraphs does that hurt throughput under high concurrency?

[17:10] Miles Ortega: slightly. cudagraphs reduce kernel launch overhead and improve throughput at high concurrency. disabling them keeps latency more stable on volatile memory workloads but shifts the latency distribution slightly up. it's a trade.

[18:00] Aisha Khan: we want as little correctness risk as possible. accuracy is non-negotiable. is there a way to test compatibility without full production rollout?

[18:20] Miles Ortega: yes — we can run a "kernel-compat" pass: we replay representative inferences with a debug shim that probes whether the fused TRT kernels are compatible with the model/quantization. it reports a per-kernel compatibility matrix. that way you can lock to TRT only for the kernels that are green.

[19:05] Tomás Ruiz: good. what about driver and CUDA versions? could upgrading help?

[19:28] Kavita Das: sometimes newer drivers handle pinned allocations more stably, but they can also change behavior in unexpected ways. we recommend testing captures across candidate driver versions. our runbook will include driver pinned allocation checks.

[20:30] Laura Chen: ok let's annote a triage plan. Miles?

[20:40] Miles Ortega: triage plan (high-level):
1) Deterministic capture: run pre-capture on your private cluster with our helper that pins a large slab and runs three iterations to verify address stability.
2) Compatibility pass: run kernel-compat probing to see which fused TRT kernels are usable for your q4_k variant.
3) Prefetch tuning: test slab allocation vs default prefetch, and run a KV churn simulation.
4) Bench: three-config microbenchmark (A: hosted-optimized with TRT preference; B: private-default; C: private with fixed-slab prefetch + TRT-lock for compatible kernels).
we'll collect nvprof / Nsight system traces and a condensed timeline.

[22:05] Priya Nair: how invasive is the slab pin approach? security concerns in our environment require least-privilege.

[22:30] Miles Ortega: slab pin is a user-space malloc pattern; it doesn't require kernel changes. it does require the process to have permission to mlock/pin pages — often allowed for container runtimes but some locked-down nodes require an admin tweak. we'll provide a minimal RBAC note.

[23:40] Benji Lee: on quantization—if we move to int8 and TRT supports it natively, does that remove the fallback?

[24:05] Miles Ortega: possibly. if TRT has a native int8 fused kernel for the operator shape/scale, it will pick it and remain on the TRT path. however int8 calibration errors can impact accuracy. we recommend a small A/B accuracy sweep on a curated eval set before switching.

[25:20] Priya Nair: can you walk through an example trace?

[25:40] Miles Ortega: yes, uploaded one earlier. quick walkthrough: at 00:00:03 the request hits and the runtime chooses TRT-fused for attention forward. at 00:00:04 there's a KV prefetch thread that allocates a pinned staging buffer; the buffer's address differs from what capture used, triggering cudagraph invalidation at 00:00:05. at 00:00:06 the runtime replays the graph — capture phase takes ~4ms — you can see a latency spike at 00:00:07.

[27:10] Tomás Ruiz: is there any way to make captures resilient to address change?

[27:34] Miles Ortega: one pattern is to capture with address-agnostic replay using CUDA's virtual addressing in some drivers, but that's fragile and not universally supported. better is to keep the capture environment stable (pin slabs) or avoid capturing sequences that touch volatile buffers.

[29:00] Aisha Khan: what about monitoring? we want to detect early instead of waiting for customer reports.

[29:20] Laura Chen: we recommend adding an instrumentation point in the console: an address-stability metric and graph-recapture counter per model-route. we'll ship a dashboard tile that shows recapture rate and per-route p95 spikes. Kavita will own a sample alerting threshold suggestion.

[30:15] Kavita Das: suggested alert: if graph-recapture_count > 1% over a 5-minute window or if p95 increases by >30% compared to baseline, raise P1 for triage.

[31:02] Benji Lee: on logging volume — will these extra traces create a lot of telemetry?

[31:22] Miles Ortega: they can; our runbook includes an option to do a condensed timeline export with only timestamps of recapture events and aggregate kernel-path counters rather than full nvprof dumps. that'll be enough for root cause in most cases.

[32:10] Priya Nair: ok, let's talk schedule. we want the initial microbench next week. can you run from our cluster?

[32:30] Laura Chen: yes — security-approved access is needed. Priya, can you open a support ticket with an SSH key for the CE team? that will let us run the deterministic captures.

[33:05] Priya Nair: noted. we'll open ticket after this call.

[33:20] Miles Ortega: one more edge case we found in lab: combining CUDA graph capture with mixed-precision quantization (some layers in q4_k others in fp16) increases the chance of kernel-path divergence because the scheduler does path selection per-layer. heterogeneous quantization increases the kernel compatibility matrix complexity.

[34:45] Tomás Ruiz: that is exactly our production setup — mixed q4_k + fp16. so that explains it.

[35:10] Laura Chen: ok then the compatibility pass is high priority. Miles will run the kernel-compat probe and we'll run the slab prefetch test.

[36:00] Aisha Khan: how confident are you that this will fix it?

[36:20] Miles Ortega: high confidence that pinning and kernel compatibility verification will reduce recaptures drastically. some residual jitter may persist due to NUMA and OS page reclaim; we'll quantify that in the microbench. absolute elimination isn't guaranteed but reduction from 2-3x spikes to <1.3x is achievable in many cases.

[37:10] Kavita Das: also suggested long-term: runtime enhancement to detect imminent address churn and preemptively switch to a conservative path for a few iterations rather than triggering a full capture. that's a development item but is on our roadmap.

[38:45] Benji Lee: ok, for acceptance criteria for Aureum — what should success look like for the pilot?

[39:05] Laura Chen: success criteria suggestion:
- p95 reduction for affected routes by >40% compared to current baseline
- recapture_count < 0.5% over a 24-hour run
- no accuracy regression on our curated eval set
if we hit these, move to phased rollout.

[40:30] Priya Nair: sounds reasonable. we'll target that as the go/no-go.

[41:00] Miles Ortega: logistics: I'll attach the microbench harness (Python + minimal container) and the kernel-compat shim to the ticket. the harness will run the three-config benchmark and upload condensed timelines.

[42:10] Laura Chen: are there any other blockers?

[42:35] Tomás Ruiz: admin on a couple of nodes needs to allow mlock. I'll coordinate with infra. also need to confirm GPU driver compatibility windows.

[43:00] Priya Nair: we'll aim to have infra changes by 2027-05-06.

[43:25] Aisha Khan: ok last thing — cost implications if we keep TRT locked or disable cudagraphs?

[43:50] Miles Ortega: rough ballpark: keeping TRT locked when compatible reduces token cost ~15-25% due to faster median and better throughput. disabling cudagraphs raises per-token compute overhead ~5-12% depending on concurrency. the paper-tradeoff for Aureum: slight median increase vs high tail stability.

[45:20] Benji Lee: can Redwood run a cost simulation?

[45:40] Laura Chen: yes we'll include cost delta in the microbench report. Miles will provide numbers and Kavita will include an annotated cost table.

[46:05] Tomás Ruiz: great. thanks. any more questions?

[46:18] Priya Nair: none right now. looking forward to the runbook.

[46:30] Laura Chen: ok recap of next steps: 1) Priya opens support ticket with SSH key and sanitized model snapshot (by 2027-05-05), 2) Miles runs kernel-compat probe and shares results (by 2027-05-06), 3) Redwood runs deterministic capture microbench (by 2027-05-11) and shares condensed traces + cost delta.

[47:10] Kavita Das: I'll also ship the slab allocation script and RBAC note.

[47:35] Aisha Khan: please include an explicit playbook for rolling back if accuracy issues show up.

[48:00] Miles Ortega: yes, we'll include a rollback flag that re-enables dynamic fallback and toggles TRT preference per-kernel.

[48:30] Laura Chen: thanks everyone — we'll send notes and the attachments. meeting adjourned.
